title: Note: from readable codebooks to growing them
summary: A one-day synthesis of J-space, read/write duality, recurrent transport, control theory and the older residue/probe line. The note sharpens the target from using a fixed language codebook to asking how a system can grow one: fast provisional bindings, reusable conceptual operators, slow consolidation, and external tests that decide which candidate concepts deserve to become stable primitives. Its only executable receipt is toy linear algebra; no real-model or human-neuroscience result is claimed.

nodes.claim: Asks what properties let language become a reusable computational codebook, then pushes one step further: how can a language-using dynamical system create, test and consolidate new conceptual primitives rather than only address a fixed codebook?
nodes.survived: The note separates reading from writing and records the exact idealized transport relation T = S^{-T}: J-CoT's pulled-back read-coordinate transport and an effect-preserving write transport are dual rather than generally identical. It also turns 'codebook growth' into a falsifiable program: distinguish temporary in-context bindings from stable reusable concepts, compare language-aligned sparse selection against matched non-language bases, and require candidate concepts to survive prediction/intervention/world checks before consolidation.
nodes.killed: The toy random-matrix receipt says nothing about the magnitude of T-versus-S disagreement in Qwen or any production model. The note does not establish that human concepts are literal vector directions, that J-space is phenomenal consciousness, that J-CoT's reported gains replicate, or that an elastic codebook has been built. Its developmental, Vygotskian, resonance and human-language parallels remain hypotheses or analogies until measured.

edges.why: ReadWrite made measurement and intervention separate operators and asked what a bounded read can recover only after a designed write. Note returns to that seam through J-space and Park-style probe/steer duality, now asking whether language-defined read coordinates are also good write and recurrent-state coordinates.

Note explicitly reuses the AdaptiveObserverCache lesson that a direction can be a strong sensor yet a poor control point. That earlier frozen-Qwen result becomes a concrete antecedent for the note's distinction between readable concepts, writable concepts and useful recurrent state.

Luotain already treated candidate structure as provisional until counterexamples or a theorem prover answer back. Note generalizes that discipline to codebook growth: language may propose a new primitive, but external proof, measurement or intervention must decide whether it earns consolidation.

motifs.title: A codebook is useful only if it can be read, written, reused and revised
motifs.description: ReadWrite separates observation from intervention; AdaptiveObserverCache shows that sensing and causal control can diverge inside a frozen transformer; Luotain routes unresolved residue to an external discriminator; Note joins those lines into an open question about concept acquisition. A mature language-native primitive should be addressable, causally usable, transportable across computation and revisable when the world or a proof checker says no. The human-like step still missing from ordinary frozen inference is consolidation: turning a provisional binding into a new stable operator-compatible entry.
